This version reflects a deliberate strategic simplification. The key changes from v2.0:

- Product positioning clarified: Breakaway is a data aggregator and plan adjuster, not a from-scratch AI plan generator. Race-specific coaching templates are selected at onboarding, then adjusted daily by the AI based on incoming data.
- Plan approach confirmed as Option A — Template Library: Breakaway maintains a curated library of race-specific plan templates (e.g. Berkeley Hills Road Race, flat criterium, gravel 100-miler). The AI adjusts workouts within these templates based on wearable inputs. It does not generate periodization from scratch.

- Onboarding redesigned as a structured questionnaire: a defined sequence of race and fitness questions anchors the experience from session one and populates the Athlete Profile.
- Race-specific plan library introduced: each supported race type maps to a template with documented energy system demands. Berkeley Hills Road Race fully specified as the first template.
- Athlete Data Layer formally specified as the primary technical moat: a structured, queryable store of all inputs and training rides designed to pass only relevant context to Claude, minimising token burn and prompt confusion.

- AI role clarified and bounded: Claude receives structured data summaries and returns targeted plan adjustments and coaching notes. Raw data is never passed directly. Claude never generates periodization plans from scratch.

Amateur cyclists training seriously for races face a compounding fragmentation problem: body data lives in Whoop, training load lives in Strava, nutrition is scattered, and the coaching plan lives in a PDF or a TrainerRoad calendar. No platform synthesises these signals into concrete, daily adjustments to an actual training plan.

Breakaway solves this by acting as an intelligent data aggregator and plan adjuster. The athlete selects their target race through a structured onboarding questionnaire. Breakaway assigns a proven, race-specific coaching template. Every day, it pulls data from connected wearables, evaluates it against the template, and through Max — its AI coaching layer — recommends specific adjustments in plain English. The athlete follows a real plan, not a stream of generic suggestions.

Critically, the plan is not generated by AI from scratch. It is a battle-tested template, curated by domain experts, that the AI makes smarter by adjusting it to the individual athlete's daily reality. This distinction matters: it is faster to build, easier to validate, lower in hallucination risk, and more trustworthy to the user.

The defensible moat is not the integrations — those are replicable. The moat is the Athlete Data Layer: a structured, queryable store of every wearable input and training ride, purpose-built to feed Claude only the precise context it needs. Over time, this layer builds a longitudinal model of the athlete that no competitor can replicate on day one.

> [!note] One-line positioning
> Breakaway aggregates your wearable data, maps it to a race-specific coaching template, and tells you exactly what to change — today.

A competitive amateur cyclist today uses multiple disconnected tools, each doing one thing well in isolation:

| Tool | What It Does Well | What It Cannot Do |
|---|---|---|
| TrainerRoad | Structured workouts, FTP progression, plan templates | Knows nothing about your recovery, nutrition, or life this week |
| Whoop | HRV, sleep staging, recovery score | Has no idea what your plan says or whether today's workout is appropriate |
| Garmin Connect | Power data, training load, VO₂ Max trend | Cannot adjust the plan based on how recovered you are |
| Strava | Activity history, segment data, TSS | No coaching layer, no plan intelligence, no recommendations |
| Nutrition apps | Calorie and macro logging | Completely disconnected from training demands or race timing |

The athlete is manually doing the synthesis that a coach would do: reading across all these tools, deciding whether today's planned workout still makes sense, and making a call. This is cognitively expensive and most athletes get it wrong.

What is absent is not more data. Athletes have more data than they can process. What is absent is a layer that sits above the data and translates it into a single, actionable daily recommendation tied to a specific race goal. That is the job Breakaway does.

chunks.section: 2. Problem Statement > 2.3 Why Race-Specific Plans Matter
chunks.text: Generic training plans are built for an average athlete with an average race. Berkeley Hills Road Race is not average. It is three laps of sustained threshold climbing followed by a VO₂ Max sprint to the line. A plan built for a flat criterium will produce an athlete who is fast but cannot sustain power for 20 minutes on a climb. Race-specific templates fix this at the foundation.

Primary user: A competitive amateur cyclist preparing for a target road race or gran fondo. Trains 8–12 hours per week. Uses at least one of Whoop, Garmin, or Strava. Has a plan — either from TrainerRoad, a coach PDF, or a generic online source — but has no reliable way to adjust it in real time based on how their body is actually responding. Wants one clear answer every morning: should I do what the plan says today, and if not, what instead?

To be the intelligent layer between an athlete's wearable data and their coaching plan — making every serious amateur's training as adaptive and race-specific as if they had a professional coach reviewing their data every morning.

Breakaway is a data aggregator and plan adjuster. It is not a training app, a social platform, or a workout library. It is the AI layer that makes a proven coaching plan responsive to the actual athlete following it.

The plan is predetermined and race-specific. The intelligence is in the daily adjustment. The moat is the structured data layer that makes those adjustments increasingly precise over time.

The onboarding questionnaire is the foundation of everything Breakaway does. It is not a settings screen. It is a structured intake that populates the Athlete Profile, selects the correct coaching template, and gives Max the context needed to make every subsequent recommendation meaningful.

The questionnaire is completed once at setup, with individual fields updateable later. It is designed to take under 5 minutes. Every question has a direct downstream effect on the plan or the coaching logic — nothing is collected that is not used.

> [!note] Design principle
> No question appears in the onboarding flow unless its answer changes the coaching output. If removing a question would not change anything Max does, the question does not belong here.

chunks.section: 4. Race-Specific Onboarding Questionnaire > 4.1 Question Sequence > Block 1: Race Target
chunks.text:
These questions select the coaching template and set the entire training objective.

| Question | Input Type | How It Is Used |
|---|---|---|
| What is your target race? | Dropdown from supported race library, or manual entry | Selects the coaching template. Each supported race has a documented energy system profile. |
| What is the race date? | Date picker | Sets the training timeline. Determines number of build weeks, taper start, and race week protocol activation. |
| Is this your A-race (peak priority) or a B/C-race? | Single select: A / B / C | A-race gets full taper and race week protocol. B/C-races are trained through or with partial taper. |

chunks.section: 4. Race-Specific Onboarding Questionnaire > 4.1 Question Sequence > Block 1: Race Target
chunks.text:
| Question | Input Type | How It Is Used |
|---|---|---|
| Have you done this race before? | Yes / No | If yes, prompts for prior finish time and any notes. Feeds into the race strategy pacing model. |

chunks.section: 4. Race-Specific Onboarding Questionnaire > 4.1 Question Sequence > Block 2: Current Fitness
chunks.text:
These questions calibrate the template intensity to the athlete's actual fitness level.

| Question | Input Type | How It Is Used |
|---|---|---|
| Do you know your current FTP (Functional Threshold Power)? | Yes → number entry. No → skip. | Primary intensity calibrator. All training zones and workout targets are expressed as % of FTP. If unknown, estimated from RPE data in first 2 weeks. |
| How many hours per week can you train? | Number slider (4–16 hrs) | Sets total weekly training stress budget. Determines which template volume tier is assigned. |
| Which days are you available to train? | Multi-select day picker | Distributes template workouts across available days. Hard days are not placed on consecutive days unless unavoidable. |

chunks.section: 4. Race-Specific Onboarding Questionnaire > 4.1 Question Sequence > Block 2: Current Fitness
chunks.text:
| Question | Input Type | How It Is Used |
|---|---|---|
| What is your experience level? | Beginner / Intermediate / Advanced / Category racer | Modifies template intensity and workout complexity. Beginners receive fewer VO₂ Max sessions; advanced athletes receive more race-specific specificity. |

chunks.section: 4. Race-Specific Onboarding Questionnaire > 4.1 Question Sequence > Block 3: Connected Platforms
chunks.text:
These questions determine which data sources are available, which in turn determines the confidence level of Max’s recommendations.

| Question | Input Type | How It Is Used |
|---|---|---|
| Which platforms do you use? | Visual checkbox menu with device logos | Triggers OAuth connection flow for each selected platform. Determines which data dimensions have high vs. low confidence signals. |
| Do you train with a power meter? | Yes / No | If yes, TSS is power-based (more accurate). If no, TSS is estimated from HR. This affects how conservatively Max interprets training load. |
| Do you have a Whoop? | Yes (already selected above) / No | If no, recovery signal falls back to Garmin body battery or manual 1–10 slider. Max communicates lower confidence in recovery recommendations. |

chunks.section: 4. Race-Specific Onboarding Questionnaire > 4.1 Question Sequence > Block 4: Race-Specific Context
chunks.text:
These questions appear only for the athlete’s selected race type and feed the race strategy engine.

| Question | Input Type | How It Is Used |
|---|---|---|
| What is your goal for this race? | Dropdown: Finish / Top half of field / Podium / Personal best time / Specific finish time | Sets the ambition level. Affects pacing targets, how conservatively the taper is managed, and the race strategy framing. |
| Do you have the course GPX file? | Upload (optional) | If uploaded, Max parses gradient and identifies key climb profiles. If not uploaded, the template uses the pre-loaded course profile from the race library. |

chunks.section: 4. Race-Specific Onboarding Questionnaire > 4.1 Question Sequence > Block 4: Race-Specific Context
chunks.text:
| Question | Input Type | How It Is Used |
|---|---|---|
| Any injuries or physical limitations we should know about? | Free text (optional) | Feeds into Max’s context. High-impact injuries (hamstring, knee) suppress certain workout types in the recommendation logic. |
| How would you describe your biggest limiter? | Dropdown: Sustained climbing / Short punchy efforts / Endurance / Sprint / All-around | Adds a second layer of specificity to workout selection within the template. A climber with poor sprint will receive more anaerobic work than the base template. |

The template library is the coaching foundation of Breakaway. Each template is a race-specific, periodized training block built by domain experts for a defined race profile. The AI does not generate these plans — it selects and adjusts them.

> [!note] Option A confirmed
> Templates are pre-built by coaches or domain experts and stored in the system. The AI's role is to select the correct template at onboarding and make daily adjustments to it based on incoming data. This approach is faster to build, easier to validate, and more trustworthy to users than AI-generated periodization.

chunks.section: 5. Coaching Plan Template Library > 5.1 Template Selection Logic
chunks.text:
At the end of onboarding, Breakaway selects a template using a two-step process:

- Step 1 — Race type match: the target race is mapped to a race profile category (sustained climbing road race, flat criterium, rolling gran fondo, punchy circuit race, gravel endurance). Each category has one or more templates.
- Step 2 — Volume tier match: the template is scaled to the athlete’s available weekly hours. Templates exist in three tiers: Low (4–8 hrs/week), Mid (8–12 hrs/week), High (12–16 hrs/week). The correct tier is selected automatically from the onboarding answer.

The selected template is displayed to the athlete with a plain-English explanation of why it was chosen and what it is designed to achieve.

chunks.section: 5. Coaching Plan Template Library > 5.2 Template Structure
chunks.text:
Every template follows the same periodization architecture:

| Phase | Duration | Primary Objective | Dominant Workout Types |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base | Weeks 1–3 | Aerobic foundation, fatigue resistance | Zone 2 endurance, sweet spot, aerobic tempo |
| Build | Weeks 4–6 | Race-specific intensity, threshold development | Threshold intervals, sustained climbing simulation |
| Speciality | Weeks 7–8 | Peak race-specific fitness | VO₂ Max, race-pace efforts, climbing repeats |
| Taper | Week 9 (race −7 to race day) | Freshness, activation, race readiness | Short intensity, activation rides, openers |
| Recovery | Embedded every 4th week | Adaptation, injury prevention | Zone 1–2, reduced volume, mobility |

The daily experience is the product. Every other feature exists to make this moment better. The athlete opens Breakaway each morning and gets one clear answer: here is what the plan says, here is what your body says, and here is what I recommend.

chunks.section: 6. Daily Coaching Experience > 6.1 Training Readiness Score
chunks.text:
A single 0–100 score synthesising all available signals into one daily verdict. Displayed as the hero element of the dashboard, with a GO HARD / MODIFIED / RECOVER verdict.

| Input Signal | Weight | Source | Fallback if Unavailable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recovery / HRV | 45% | Whoop (primary), Garmin body battery (secondary) | Manual 1–10 slider, on-demand only — never prompted |
| Training Load Balance | 35% | CTL vs. ATL from Strava + Garmin power data | Strava HR-based estimate |
| Nutrition / Carb Availability | 20% | Native macro logger | Estimated from training load if nothing logged |

chunks.section: 6. Daily Coaching Experience > 6.1 Training Readiness Score
chunks.text: The score is recalculated live when nutrition is logged. Max’s recommendation is gated by the score: a score below 50 suppresses hard workouts regardless of what the template prescribes for that day.

chunks.section: 6. Daily Coaching Experience > 6.2 Max Coaching Note
chunks.text:
Two sentences, delivered every morning, directly below the readiness score. The first sentence states what was planned and what is being recommended instead (if different). The second sentence gives the one most important reason why.

> Planned: Galena — 90 min threshold. Today’s recommendation: Pettit — 60 min Zone 2.
> Your Whoop recovery is 61% and you’ve accumulated 412 TSS this week — going hard today risks the quality of Saturday’s key session.

If the plan is unchanged, the note confirms this and briefly explains what today’s workout is building toward in the context of the race:

> On track: Galena — 90 min threshold, as planned.
> This session simulates the sustained climbing demand of Wildcat Canyon — three weeks out, this is exactly the stimulus you need.

chunks.section: 6. Daily Coaching Experience > 6.3 Contextual Reply Chips
chunks.text:
Below the coaching note, Max surfaces 3 dynamically generated follow-up prompts based on today’s actual data. These are generated by Claude alongside the coaching note as a structured JSON field, ensuring they are always relevant to what Max just said.

- Tier 1 — Daily contextual chips: generated from today’s data (e.g. “Why Zone 2 today?” appears only because recovery is flagged)
- Tier 2 — Follow-on chips: appear after Max responds to guide the next question
- Tier 3 — Persistent utility chips: always available via scroll — Week ahead, Race readiness, Fuelling plan, Adjust schedule

Maximum 3 chips visible at any time.

chunks.section: 6. Daily Coaching Experience > 6.4 Full Chat with Max
chunks.text: Tapping the coaching note opens a full conversational interface with Max. Max has access to the athlete’s structured data context for the session and can answer detailed questions about the plan, the race, fuelling, or any adjustment. All previous sessions are summarised in the Athlete Data Layer and available as context.

chunks.section: 6. Daily Coaching Experience > 6.5 Manual Sleep Input
chunks.text: Available on-demand for users without a sleep tracker. Accessible via a single tap from the dashboard. Never proactively prompted. Asks only two questions: hours slept and a 1–10 quality rating. Data is logged to the Athlete Data Layer and incorporated into the next readiness score calculation.

chunks.section: 7. Athlete Data Layer — The Technical Moat
chunks.text:
> [!note] Primary moat
> The Athlete Data Layer is Breakaway’s most defensible asset. It is a structured, queryable store of every input and training ride, purpose-built to pass only the precise context Claude needs for each query. This minimises token burn, eliminates prompt confusion, and compounds in value with every week of use.

chunks.section: 7. Athlete Data Layer — The Technical Moat > 7.1 Why This Architecture Matters
chunks.text:
Most AI fitness products fail at the data layer. They either pass everything into a single large prompt (expensive, slow, and confusing to the model) or pass nothing useful (producing generic advice). Neither is acceptable at scale or in a real product.

Breakaway solves this by treating the athlete’s data as a structured database, not a conversation history. Claude is never asked to reason across raw API responses. It receives a compressed, purpose-built context object assembled from the Athlete Data Layer immediately before each query. The result is faster responses, lower costs, and more precise coaching.

chunks.section: 7. Athlete Data Layer — The Technical Moat > 7.3 Claude Prompting Architecture
chunks.text:
This is the critical design decision that separates Breakaway from naive AI fitness products. Claude is never given a raw data dump. It receives a structured prompt assembled from pre-computed context summaries. A typical daily coaching query looks like this:

```text
ATHLETE PROFILE (static)
FTP: 250W | Race: Berkeley Hills Road Race | Date: April 26 | Weeks out: 3 | Goal: Top half of field | Limiter: Sustained climbing

DAILY CONTEXT (from daily_inputs, computed)
Readiness: 61/100 (MODIFIED) | Recovery: Whoop 61% HRV 52ms [HIGH confidence] | Sleep: 7.2h [HIGH confidence] | Carbs: 148g / 290g target [LOW confidence — manual] | CTL: 68 | ATL: 74 | TSB: -6

PLAN CONTEXT
Planned today: Galena — 90min threshold (TSS 95) | Phase: Speciality Week 1 | Template: Berkeley Hills Mid-Volume

chunks.section: 7. Athlete Data Layer — The Technical Moat > 7.3 Claude Prompting Architecture
chunks.text:
MEMORY DIGEST
Compliance: 82% over last 4 weeks. Tends to under-fuel on hard days. No injury flags active.

QUERY
Generate today’s coaching note (2 sentences max) and 3 contextual reply chip suggestions (JSON array). If readiness < 65, recommend a modified workout from the template’s approved substitution list.
```

This prompt structure has several deliberate properties:

- Context is always labelled by type and confidence level — Max knows when to hedge
- Raw numbers are never passed without interpretation (e.g. CTL/ATL are given, not the full 42-day time series)
- The query is bounded: Max is asked to do one specific thing, not ‘analyse my training’

chunks.section: 7. Athlete Data Layer — The Technical Moat > 7.3 Claude Prompting Architecture
chunks.text:
- Token count is predictable and capped: the daily context prompt is approximately 350–450 tokens regardless of how much underlying data exists
- Claude never touches the database directly — only the pre-assembled context objects

chunks.section: 7. Athlete Data Layer — The Technical Moat > 7.4 Longitudinal Memory — The Compounding Moat
chunks.text:
The memory_digest object is what transforms Breakaway from a tool into a coaching relationship. It is updated weekly by a background process that analyses the training_rides and daily_inputs tables and extracts meaningful patterns:

- Compliance patterns: which days and workout types the athlete consistently completes or skips
- Physiological response curves: how many days HRV takes to recover after different effort types
- Fuelling tendencies: days where calorie/carb intake correlates with poor performance
- Race history: complete record of each race with pre-race plan, actual power file, and outcome

chunks.section: 7. Athlete Data Layer — The Technical Moat > 7.4 Longitudinal Memory — The Compounding Moat
chunks.text:
The memory_digest is compressed to under 200 tokens but contains the most diagnostically relevant patterns for the current training context. A race-week session gets race history and taper patterns. A recovery day session gets fatigue response curves.

This is the switching cost. Rebuilding this digest from scratch takes 6–8 weeks of data. No competitor who acquires a new user has it on day one.

Race strategy and fuelling guidance are delivered in the lead-up to the target race. This is one of the most differentiated features in Breakaway — no existing platform synthesises current fitness, course demands, and individual data into a concrete, personalised race plan.

chunks.section: 8. Race & Fuelling Strategy > 8.1 Pre-Race Plan (Generated 5–7 Days Before Race)
chunks.text:
Max generates a race plan document the athlete can print or screenshot and take to the start line. It is populated from the race_context summary object and the athlete’s current fitness data:

- Target watts by course segment, expressed as % of current FTP
- Pacing strategy narrative: where to conserve, where to push, where this specific race is typically won
- Key decision points by kilometre or mile marker
- Weather note if race-day forecast is available

Example output — Berkeley Hills Road Race:

chunks.section: 8. Race & Fuelling Strategy > 8.1 Pre-Race Plan (Generated 5–7 Days Before Race)
chunks.text: > Your CTL is 71, TSB is +4 — you’re in good form. Target 87% FTP on Wildcat Canyon (laps 1 and 2). Sit in for the first 10 miles; the pace will feel easy — let it. The race fractures at the base of lap 3’s climb. That’s your moment. Push to 93% FTP from the bottom and do not respond to attacks before KM 28. The sprint on South Park Drive is 3–5 minutes — treat it as a VO₂ Max effort, everything you have left.

Max generates a personalised fuelling schedule based on race duration estimate, individual carb metabolism patterns from the nutrition log history, and standard endurance fuelling guidelines. It is expressed in concrete, practical terms:

- Pre-race meal: timing, carbohydrate target, example foods
- On-bike fuelling: gel and bottle timing by approximate race time (e.g. first gel at 45 minutes, carb bottle sips every 20 minutes)
- Target carbohydrate intake per hour during the race
- Post-race recovery nutrition window and targets

Example:

> Race morning — 3 hours before: 120g carbs. 15 min before gun: 1 gel. On bike: gel at 45 min, gel at 1:20, carb bottle throughout. Target 65g carbs/hour once underway. You tend to under-fuel on hard days — set a phone reminder for each gel.
The final sentence of the fuelling plan example above (“you tend to under-fuel”) is drawn from the memory_digest. This is the feature that makes it feel like a real coach — one who has been watching.

chunks.section: 8. Race & Fuelling Strategy > 8.3 Race Week Protocol (Activates 7 Days Before Race)
chunks.text:
Day-by-day taper guidance for the final week:

| Day | Focus | Max’s Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Race −7 (Mon) | Final quality session | Short threshold effort — maintain sharpness, do not add fatigue. Galena − 2 or equivalent. |
| Race −6 (Tue) | Active recovery | Zone 1 spin, 30–45 min. Legs only, no efforts. |
| Race −5 (Wed) | Race openers | Short VO₂ Max efforts — 3x3 min at 110% FTP. Wake the engine. |
| Race −4 (Thu) | Rest | Complete rest or gentle walk. Prioritise sleep. |
| Race −3 (Fri) | Travel / logistics | Rest. Recon the course start area if possible. Carb loading begins tonight. |
| Race −2 (Sat) | Activation | 20–30 min easy spin with 3x30 sec race-pace efforts. Bike check. |
| Race −1 (Sun) | Rest | Rest completely. Final carb-loading meal. Sleep priority. |

chunks.section: 8. Race & Fuelling Strategy > 8.3 Race Week Protocol (Activates 7 Days Before Race)
chunks.text:
| Day | Focus | Max’s Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Race Day | Execute the plan | Follow the pre-race plan. Trust the build. |

After the race, Max detects the Strava activity (flagged as race type by duration and effort level) and generates a brief analysis:

- Power file vs. pre-race plan: where execution matched, where it deviated
- Identified limiters from the data: fitness ceiling, fuelling issue, tactical errors, pacing
- Key learnings stored in the memory_digest for the next race cycle

Each completed race makes the next race plan smarter. This is the flywheel.

When multiple sources provide data for the same dimension, a defined hierarchy governs which signal is used. Signal selection is based on published accuracy research, product market sentiment, and what each platform was built to optimise for.

| Dimension | Primary | Secondary | Fallback | Rationale |

chunks.section: 9. Data Integrations > 9.3 Why Strava Is the Right Primary Pipe (Phase 1)
chunks.text: Strava acts as a universal aggregator for training data, making it more valuable than a direct Garmin integration for Phase 1: Garmin auto-syncs every activity to Strava, so pulling from Strava captures all Garmin data without the Garmin approval process. TrainerRoad completed workouts also auto-sync to Strava, meaning Breakaway sees actual workout completion without any TrainerRoad API dependency. In Phase 2, Garmin direct integration adds VO₂ Max trending and independent HRV data.

| Layer | Technology | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Frontend | React + Tailwind CSS | Fast prototyping, mobile-friendly, component-based |
| Backend | Node.js / Express | JavaScript consistency, strong API ecosystem |
| Database | PostgreSQL | Relational structure for Athlete Data Layer, training plans, time-series inputs |
| AI Layer | Claude API (Sonnet) | Coaching notes, plan adjustments, race strategy, reply chip generation |
| Athlete Data Layer | PostgreSQL + nightly background jobs | Structured context summaries computed nightly and on-demand |
| Template Library | JSON flat file (Phase 1) → PostgreSQL (Phase 2) | Race-specific coaching templates with workout assignments by phase and week |

| Layer | Technology | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Workout DB | JSON flat file | ~100 TrainerRoad workouts mapped by zone, duration, adaptation, link |
| Auth | OAuth 2.0 | Required for Whoop, Strava, Garmin, Google Calendar |
| Hosting | Vercel (frontend) + Railway (backend) | Simple deployment for MVP |

The data flow is designed to keep Claude’s context clean and predictable:

- Wearable APIs (Whoop, Strava) push or are polled nightly. Data is written to daily_inputs and training_rides tables.
- Background jobs recompute context_summaries nightly: daily_context, weekly_context, race_context, memory_digest, nutrition_context.
- On user open, the app reads the pre-computed daily_context summary and displays the dashboard. No Claude call is made at this point.
- When the coaching note is requested (either automatically each morning or manually), the backend assembles the structured prompt from the relevant context summaries and makes a single Claude API call.

- Claude returns a JSON response: coaching_note (string, max 2 sentences), modified_workout (object or null), reply_chips (array of 3 strings).
- The response is cached for the day. Subsequent chat messages with Max use the cached coaching note as context and extend the conversation without re-fetching summaries.

Token efficiency is a first-class design constraint. The target is a predictable, capped prompt size regardless of how much underlying data exists:

| Context Object | Estimated Tokens | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Athlete profile (static) | ~80 tokens | Rarely changes. Cached. |
| Daily context | ~120 tokens | Recomputed nightly. |
| Weekly context | ~80 tokens | Recomputed nightly. |
| Race context | ~100 tokens | Changes only as race approaches. |
| Memory digest | ~150 tokens | Compressed pattern summary. Updated weekly. |
| Query instruction | ~50 tokens | Specific, bounded task description. |
| Total daily coaching prompt | ~580 tokens | Well within efficient range. Leaves ample room for Claude’s response. |

For longer conversational sessions (full chat with Max), the conversation history is passed in addition to the context objects. A hard cap of 4,000 tokens total per session is enforced. Older conversation turns are summarised and replaced rather than dropped raw.

> [!note] Phase discipline
> Phase 1 must be validated before Phase 2 begins. The north star: 20 users open Breakaway every morning for 30 consecutive days. If that is achieved, every feature on the Phase 2 and 3 roadmap is justified. If not, the question is why — before anything else is built.

- Template accuracy: coaching templates must be reviewed by a domain expert (coach or experienced racer) before beta launch. AI-generated template errors are not acceptable.
- Template staleness: as athletes’ fitness evolves, the template intensity may need recalibration. An FTP re-test prompt at weeks 4 and 8 is the initial mitigation.
- Nutrition advice liability: coaching notes framed as suggestions, not medical advice. Disclaimer in onboarding.
- Cold start confidence: in the first 1–2 weeks, the memory_digest is sparse. Max must communicate appropriate confidence levels. “I’m still learning your patterns — check back in after a few more rides.”

chunks.section: 12. Risks & Open Questions > 12.3 Key Decisions Still Open
chunks.text:
- Pricing: free personal tool vs. freemium vs. $12–15/month subscription?
- Mobile-first vs. web-first: dashboard suits desktop; daily coaching note and race day reference suits mobile.
- Template curation process: who builds and validates the templates? Founder only for Phase 1, or bring in an experienced coach as an advisor?
- FTP estimation: for users who don’t know their FTP, what is the onboarding protocol? RPE-based estimation ride, or a deferred first-week test?

A small local web app that ran alongside a live Sleeper fantasy football draft. It tracked every pick in real time and recommended who to take next. It was built in one session with Claude Code on the day of the draft in September 2026.

The goal was a tool to use during a **12-team, full-PPR snake draft** on Sleeper, to make sure that:

1. **The right players get drafted.** Recommendations should come from expert consensus rankings, not Sleeper's ADP (average draft position), which reflects what the crowd picks rather than how good players are.
2. **Positional gaps get filled.** The app should know which starting slots are still empty and point toward them.
3. **Each pick is a good pick for that round**, not just the best player left. For example, is the 11th-ranked RB a better choice at pick 2.10 than the top-ranked TE?
4. **There's quick context on each player**: a short upside/downside note and any injury status.

Two ideas were considered:

- **Screenshot app.** Upload a screenshot of the draft board and get a suggestion. This was rejected because reading text from images is unreliable and breaks whenever Sleeper changes its layout.
- **Live companion.** This turned out to be the *easier* option. Sleeper has a **public, no-login JSON API** for drafts:
  - `GET https://api.sleeper.app/v1/draft/{draft_id}` returns draft settings, roster slots and scoring.
  - `GET https://api.sleeper.app/v1/draft/{draft_id}/picks` returns every pick made so far.

The companion won. It was built as a **single `index.html` file** with the rankings data embedded: no build step and no dependencies. A tiny Node static server (`server.js`) serves it at `http://localhost:8931`. Vercel hosting was considered and dropped in favour of running it locally.

The default rankings deliberately avoid Sleeper ADP. They blend two expert sources, both confirmed to be **full-PPR** lists:

| Source | Coverage | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| FantasyPros consensus (about 128 experts, PPR cheat sheet) | Top 100 | 0.6 |
| ESPN Field Yates PPR rankings | Top 160 | 0.4 |

- A player on both lists gets `FantasyPros_rank × 0.6 + ESPN_rank × 0.4`, and the list is re-sorted by that blended score. FantasyPros gets more weight because it is already an average of many experts.
- A player on only one list (mostly ESPN's 101–160 range) keeps that source's rank.
- The result is about 160 players, each with an overall rank, position rank and each source's individual rank.
- It's a **static snapshot** from draft day and does not refresh automatically.

**Why it differs from ADP:** ADP is crowd behaviour. It captures name recognition, hype and slow reactions to news. Expert rankings are considered opinions of each player's season value, so they usually react to trades and role changes before ADP does.

- **Live polling:** the app fetches picks every 3 seconds. Sleeper's CDN caches the picks endpoint for up to 30 seconds (`s-maxage=30`), so a new pick can take up to about 30 seconds to appear. That's well inside a 60-second pick clock.
- **Best Available:** consensus rankings with anyone already drafted by *any* team removed. It can be filtered by position and searched.
- **My Team and Needs tracker:** your own picks are detected automatically and slotted into QB/RB/WR/TE/FLEX/K/DEF, with each starting slot shown as filled or still open.
- **Value sort:** the default sort order, which adjusts consensus rank for position scarcity (see below). You can switch back to raw consensus rank.

- **Top recommendation banner:** the single best-value pick available right now (skipping K/DST), tagged "fills a need" where it applies.
- **Needs highlight:** a green edge on Best Available rows for positions (or flex-eligible positions) you still need.
- **VALUE / REACH tags:** these compare a player's consensus rank with the current pick number. They appear on Best Available before you pick, and on the Live Picks feed (last 25 picks) afterwards.
- **Player notes and injury badges:** a one-line upside/downside note per player, plus live injury status (Questionable, IR, PUP) from Sleeper's player database.
- **Bye-week clash warnings:** a flag on any available player whose bye week matches a player already on your roster.

- **Strategy panel:** short guidance on draft order. Prioritise RB/WR early, wait on QB unless an elite rushing QB falls, take either an elite TE or wait, and leave K/DST until last.
- **Settings:** set the draft ID and your draft slot. Both are saved in `localStorage`, so they survive a page refresh.

Raw consensus rank answers "who is the better player?", but not "who is the better pick right now?" The value model adds position scarcity as a *secondary nudge*:

```text
scarcity   = POS_SLOPE[pos] × (REPLACEMENT_RANK[pos] − position_rank)
blended    = −consensus_rank + 0.4 × scarcity

REPLACEMENT_RANK = { QB:14, RB:34, WR:40, TE:14, K:12, DST:12 }
POS_SLOPE        = { QB:0.6, RB:1.3, WR:1.0, TE:1.0, K:0.3, DST:0.3 }
```

- **Replacement rank** is roughly how deep you can go at a position before you're down to players any team could pick up on waivers.

- **Slope** is how much each step down the position ranks costs. RB drops off sharply after the true workhorse backs (1.3). WR declines more gradually because PPR keeps more receivers useful (1.0). QB, K and DST are cheap to stream, so a step there costs less (0.6 and 0.3).
- K and DST are always sorted below skill positions, whatever their score.
- Each row shows `#rank` and `scarcity +N` separately, so you can see *why* a player landed where they did.

It's a heuristic based on rank distance to replacement level, not true value-based drafting built on projected points, since no paid projection data was used.

chunks.section: The Value Model > How the model evolved
chunks.text:
1. **First version:** `replacement_rank − position_rank` alone. This answered the 2.10 question (it favoured the RB11 over the TE1), but it let scarcity *override* real differences in talent.
2. **K/DST bug:** late in the draft, a still-available top defense outscored deep bench RBs, which contradicted the strategy panel. The fix was to pin K and DST to the bottom.
3. **Blend fix:** an elite RB (ranked #3 overall) was scored below a WR ranked #12 overall. After the fix, consensus rank is the main signal and scarcity only adds a 0.4-weighted nudge.

chunks.section: The Value Model > How the model evolved
chunks.text: 4. **Slope fix:** because WR's replacement cutoff was deeper (40 vs 34), every WR got about 6 more scarcity points than an RB at the same depth. That flipped **13 adjacent RB-over-WR pairs**, all in the same direction. Per-position slopes removed every flip where the consensus gap was more than 5 spots. Six near-ties (gaps of 0.2–0.6 points) remain as genuine close calls.

| Bug | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "My Team" empty in mock drafts | Sleeper leaves `roster_id` null on mock-draft picks | Identify your picks by `draft_slot`, which is set in both mock and real drafts |
| Refresh reset the draft board | Draft ID was only kept in memory | Save the draft ID and slot to `localStorage` |
| VALUE/REACH labels reversed | `rank − pick_no` operands were the wrong way round | Changed to `pick_no − rank` |
| Taking Brian Robinson would also mark Bijan Robinson as taken | Name matching shortened first names to an initial ("b robinson") | Match on full normalized names |
| Drafted defenses never left Best Available | Sleeper labels them `DEF`, the rankings use `DST` | Normalize position labels |

| Bug | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong injury and experience data (e.g. Travis Etienne shown on IR; Jayden Daniels shown as a rookie) | The same initial-only matching in the offline data-enrichment script let Trevor Etienne and Jalon Daniels overwrite them | Fixed the script and re-checked all 160 players against Sleeper's data |
| Kenny Gainwell never matched as drafted | ESPN called him "Kenneth", Sleeper uses "Kenny" | Renamed him to match Sleeper |
| Wrong "rookie" / "sophomore" notes | Hand-written notes weren't checked against Sleeper's `years_exp` | Corrected 23 notes (12 second-year players, 7 third-year players, and others) |

All of the fixes were verified against a Sleeper **instant mock draft**, which works with the app exactly like a real draft.

- **Check for an API before building scraping or screenshot reading.** Sleeper's public API turned the "hard" idea into the easy one.
- **Test on a mock draft before relying on the app live.** Mock drafts showed up the `roster_id` difference and most of the other bugs before they could matter.
- **Name matching is the weakest point when joining datasets.** Shortening names to initials caused three separate bugs. Match on full names and check every player afterwards.
- **Fix a bug everywhere its logic is copied.** The matching bug was fixed in the app but left in the offline script, and it came back as wrong injury and experience data.

- **Keep heuristics secondary to consensus.** A scarcity score that overrides talent gives confident but wrong answers. Using it only as a nudge, and showing it separately, keeps the reasoning visible.
- **Expert rank vs ADP gaps are signals, not errors.** When a player's expert rank is far above their ADP, check for a recent trade or role change before treating it as a mistake.

- a recipe library
- Claude-generated recipes (gluten-free by default, with a way to turn that off)
- recipe import from websites, Instagram and cookbook photos
- week suggestions that share ingredients, so you shop smarter
- step-by-step cook cards with timers

- a simple UI where the **ingredient list gets top priority**

The folder `C:\Users\thoma\GRKN` is empty, so this is a new build.

- **Backend and sync: Convex.** Every query updates live on both phones, writes show on screen immediately and then sync, changes are transactional, and it reconnects and resends on its own. It also stores files (recipe photos) and runs the server functions that call Claude, so the Anthropic key never reaches the phone.
- **Frontend: a web app built only for iPhone** (you both use iPhones). It uses Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript + Tailwind + shadcn/ui, is installed to the home screen from Safari, and is hosted on Vercel. There is **no desktop layout**. On a computer it shows as a centred, phone-width screen.

chunks.section: iPhone-first UI rules (built in from day one, never added later)
chunks.text:
- **Screen fit:**
  - It opens full screen from the home screen, using the standard iOS home-screen app settings (status bar style, app icon, launch screens).
  - Content avoids the notch and home bar (`viewport-fit=cover`).
  - Layout uses the dynamic viewport height, so the Safari toolbar never cuts off content.
  - Background bounce is locked, so pull-to-refresh can't fight with scrolling.
- **Native patterns:**
  - a bottom tab bar that sits above the home indicator
  - bottom sheets (`vaul`) instead of pop-ups
  - swipe to delete and swipe between weeks and cook steps (`framer-motion`)
  - large titles and back navigation that feel like iOS
  - press states instead of hover effects
- **Touch:**
  - tap targets are at least 44pt
  - text fields use 16px text, so iOS doesn't zoom in

chunks.section: iPhone-first UI rules (built in from day one, never added later)
chunks.text:
- the number keypad appears for quantities
  - no action depends on hover or a right-click
  - long-press actions have a visible alternative (⋯ menu)
- **iOS limits planned around:**
  - Safari has no vibration support, so timers use sound plus push. The sound is unlocked when you tap Start, because iOS requires a tap before playing audio.
  - Keeping the screen awake needs iOS 18.4 or later in a home-screen app. It fails silently on older versions.
  - Push needs the app installed to the home screen (iOS 16.4+).
  - Web Share Target isn't supported on iOS, so Instagram and website sharing uses a **"Send to GRKN" iOS Shortcut** in the share sheet. The Shortcut opens `/create/import?url=…`. Setup is a one-tap install link from Settings. Pasting the link also works.

chunks.section: iPhone-first UI rules (built in from day one, never added later)
chunks.text:
- The camera for cookbook pages opens through a file input set to capture, and each photo is shrunk on the phone to about 1600px before upload (fewer tokens and faster).
- **Performance on a phone:**
  - lists load recipes on the server, only small interactive pieces run on the phone
  - no big libraries
  - fonts use the iPhone's own font, SF Pro (`system-ui`)
  - the app shell is saved on the phone, so it opens instantly
- **Login: Convex Auth** with an email magic link (sent through Resend) and Google. Each of you has your own account in one shared **household**, joined with a 6-character invite code.

chunks.section: iPhone-first UI rules (built in from day one, never added later)
chunks.text:
- **Gluten (coeliac-strict):** a household setting, **"Gluten-free by default: ON"**. On the generate and plan screens there's a toggle, "Include gluten this time (e.g. she's away)". Each ingredient gets `glutenRisk: none | contains | check-label`:
  - **contains** covers wheat, barley, rye, malt, regular soy sauce, standard beer, and oats unless certified GF.
  - **check-label** covers stock cubes, sauces, spice mixes, sausages, chocolate and the like.
  - Every recipe gets a `glutenFree` flag, which is true only if nothing is marked `contains`.
  - The recipe page shows a banner listing items to check, and cross-contamination notes where they apply (separate toaster or colander, flour dust).

chunks.section: iPhone-first UI rules (built in from day one, never added later)
chunks.text:
- Imported recipes are checked by Claude and flagged, and a GF swap is suggested for each problem ingredient.
  - On the shopping list, `check-label` items carry a small "GF? check label" tag.
- **Recipe images: none.** Text-only cards with a clear layout (title, time, GF badge, key ingredients). Cookbook photos are kept only as the import source.
- **Store connectivity:** signal is fine, so standard Convex sync is enough (no offline outbox).

chunks.section: Getting sync right (why this won't repeat the Firebase problem)
chunks.text:
1. **Each shopping item is its own document.** When one person ticks "milk" and the other ticks "eggs", nothing conflicts.
2. **Ticks set a value; they don't flip it.** The tick action is `setChecked(itemId, checked: boolean)`, not "toggle". If you both tap the same item, the result is still correct and stable.
3. **Instant feedback:** every tick, add and reorder shows on screen immediately and then syncs.
4. **Server-side list building:** combining the week's recipes into a shopping list happens in one transactional step on the server. Rebuilding the list keeps ticked items, manual items and edits, and only adds, removes or adjusts the items that came from recipes.

chunks.section: Getting sync right (why this won't repeat the Firebase problem)
chunks.text:
5. **Connection indicator:** a small dot shows "Live / Reconnecting / Offline – changes will sync". Changes made while offline are held and sent when you reconnect.
6. **In the store:** the shopping screen keeps the phone awake, ticked items drop to the bottom of their aisle, and each tick shows who made it ("✓ by Rory").

- `ratings` {recipeId, userId, stars 1–5, wouldCookAgain, comment?, cookedAt}: one rating per person each time you cook it
- `tasteProfile` (one per member plus a household summary) {likes[], dislikes[] (ingredients or cuisines), spiceLevel, notes, summary}: the summary is rewritten by Claude from ratings, comments and dislikes every few ratings, and is included in every generation prompt
- `pantry` {householdId, name, canonical, qty?, unit?, useSoon:boolean, addedAt}: what's on hand. Items marked `useSoon` get priority when generating and planning. Ticking a shopping item can move it into the pantry (optional). "Mark recipe cooked" offers to remove the pantry items it used up.
- `pushSubscriptions` {userId, endpoint, keys, prefs {partnerChanges, sundayNudge, timers}}

- `mealPlan` {householdId, date (YYYY-MM-DD), slot: breakfast|lunch|dinner, recipeId? | freeText?, servings, addedBy, repeatGroupId?}, indexed by household+date. `repeatGroupId` links the same breakfast repeated across several days, so editing one of them can apply to all.
- Recipes also get `mealTypes[]` (breakfast|lunch|dinner|snack) and `makeAhead:boolean`, with fridge life in days.
- `households` also gets `slotsShown` {breakfast:boolean (default off, so breakfast appears only when you turn it on), lunch, dinner}, `prepDay` (default Sunday) and `targetsByMeal` {breakfast, lunch, dinner: {proteinG, fibreG}}.
- `shoppingItems` {householdId, name, canonical, qty, unit, aisle, checked, checkedBy?, checkedAt?, sources[] {recipeId, mealPlanId}, manual:boolean, sortKey}

- `staples` {householdId, canonical}: things you always have at home (oil, salt), left off generated lists
- `aiJobs` {householdId, kind, status, input, result?, error?}: Claude calls run in the background and the screen updates live when they finish
- `weeklyBriefs` {householdId, weekStart, proteins[] (e.g. salmon, chicken, tofu), theme? ("Mexican week"), notes?, targets {proteinG, fibreG} per serving, includeGluten, createdBy}: one brief per week, kept as history so each new week can be steered away from the last few

- `planDrafts` {householdId, weekStart, briefId?, status: drafting|accepted} + `planDraftSlots` {draftId, date, slot, state: pending|suggested|kept|empty, recipeId? | card?, freeText?, nutritionEst, updatedBy}: the shared Planning board. Each slot is its own document, so the two of you can edit different slots at the same time without clashing.
- `prepPlans` {householdId, weekStart, prepDay, basedOn (fingerprint of the kept meals), stale:boolean, sessions[] {when: "Sunday" | "Wednesday top-up", totalMin, tasks[] {id, text, durationMin, timers[], forMeals[] {date, slot, recipeId}, storage ("fridge, 4 days, airtight"), doneBy?, doneAt?}}, dontPrepAhead[] {item, reason}}: the week's meal-prep guide. Tasks are ticked off live by either of you.

- `seasonalProduce` {region, month, items[] {canonical, name, peak:boolean}}: a curated table of what's in season. It's generated once per region by Claude, can be checked and edited in Settings, and is then read for free (no AI call per request).

chunks.section: Cooking nights + calendar feed (build step 8.5, after the meal prep guide)
chunks.text:
**Data model**
- `mealPlan` gets `cookMemberId?`: who is cooking that meal. Only dinners have a cook.
- `households` gets `defaultCooks` {monday…sunday: memberId?}, e.g. Rory cooks Mon and Wed. A new dinner takes the default cook for its day, and each dinner can be changed.
- `households` gets `dinnerTime` (default 19:00).
- `members` gets `calendarToken`: a secret random token for that person's calendar feed. It can be reset.

**Screens**
- **Week:** each dinner row shows the cook's initial ("R"). Tap it, or use ⋯ → "Who's cooking", to change the cook.
- **Settings → Cooking nights:** a chip per weekday to pick who cooks, and a dinner time.

chunks.section: Cooking nights + calendar feed (build step 8.5, after the meal prep guide)
chunks.text:
- **Settings → Add to Google Calendar:** a "Subscribe" button, with steps to copy the feed link and add it in Google Calendar on the web (Other calendars → From URL). There's also a "Reset link" button.

**Calendar feed** (`convex/http.ts`, `GET /cal/<token>.ics`)
- It lists only the dinners where you're the cook, for the next 3 weeks. Free-text dinners ("eating out") are left out.
- Each event is called "You're cooking: Salmon traybake". It starts at dinner time minus (prep + cook) minutes and ends at dinner time. The description holds the prep and cook minutes, the gluten status and a link to the recipe.
- Once the meal prep guide (M8) exists, the feed also includes prep sessions for whoever is doing them, e.g. "Sunday prep · ~75 min · covers 9 meals".

chunks.text:

- **Instant option:** an "Add to Google Calendar" button on each planned dinner opens a prefilled Google Calendar event (a `calendar.google.com/…action=TEMPLATE` link). It's one tap and needs no sign-in.

chunks.section: Cooking nights + calendar feed (build step 8.5, after the meal prep guide)
chunks.text: **Verification:** Rory is set to cook Mon and Wed, so new dinners on those days get Rory. The feed contains only Rory's dinners, with the right start time and duration. Changing the cook moves the dinner between the two feeds. A reset link stops the old URL from working. Once M8 exists, prep sessions appear in the feed of the person doing them.

chunks.section: Push notifications (`convex/push.ts`, with a `web-push` action and VAPID keys)
chunks.text:
- These work on iPhone (iOS 16.4+) **only once the app is installed to the home screen**. Onboarding walks you through installing, then asks for permission.
- **Partner changes:** messages are grouped so there's no spam. For example, "Rory added 4 items to the list" or "Rory planned Thursday dinner" are sent after 2 minutes with no further changes, using a Convex scheduled function. You're never notified about your own changes.
- **Prep day reminder:** the morning of your prep day, e.g. "Sunday prep: ~75 min, 9 meals covered".
- **Sunday nudge:** a Convex cron job sends "Plan next week?" at a time you choose, only if next week has empty slots.

chunks.text: - **Cook timers while the phone is locked:** starting a timer also schedules a server-side push for when it finishes (`scheduler.runAt`), and cancelling the timer cancels it. The phone also plays a sound while the app is open.

chunks.section: Claude integration (`convex/ai.ts`, a Node server function)
chunks.text:
- Uses the `@anthropic-ai/sdk` with **structured output** (tool use / JSON schema matching `recipes`) so the results are always valid, typed recipes. **Load the `claude-api` skill before writing this file.**
- **Model choice by task, to keep costs down:**
  - `claude-haiku-4-5` for cheap, mechanical jobs: normalising JSON-LD imports, tagging aisles and gluten risk, and rewriting the taste summary
  - `claude-sonnet-5` for creative jobs: generating recipes, extracting recipes from photos or text, and the overlap planner
  - no Opus by default
- **The system prompt always includes:**
  - the gluten rule, which is coeliac-strict and requires Claude to set `glutenRisk` for every ingredient
  - the household taste profile summary and dislikes (hard exclusions)

chunks.section: Claude integration (`convex/ai.ts`, a Node server function)
chunks.text:
- the top-rated and low-rated recipe titles
  - the pantry's "use soon" items
  - region and current month (for seasonality)
  - units and servings
  - recently cooked titles, to avoid repeats
  - nutrition guidance: balanced plates and vegetables in every meal

  It also asks Claude to break timers down into seconds per step and to label each ingredient with its aisle and a canonical name.
- **Keeping prompts small:**
  - The system prompt, gluten rules and output schema are fixed text, placed first with `cache_control`, so repeat calls cost about 10% of the input tokens.
  - The changing parts (profile summary, pantry, recent titles) go after the cached block and are kept short: the profile is a summary of about 150 words or less, and recent titles are capped at 20.

chunks.section: Claude integration (`convex/ai.ts`, a Node server function)
chunks.text:
- The planner receives compact ingredient lists (canonical names only), not full recipes.
  - Each task sets a tight `max_tokens`.
  - Generating returns 3 short cards first (title, one-line description, key ingredients). The full recipe is generated only for the card you pick. That's about 3× fewer output tokens than generating three complete recipes.
  - Website imports that have JSON-LD skip Claude extraction entirely and only get a Haiku pass for tagging.
- **Spend guard:** each call logs its token usage to `aiJobs`. When the monthly cap (set in Settings) is reached, new calls are refused with a friendly message. Prompt caching is used on the long system prompt and profile.

chunks.section: Claude integration (`convex/ai.ts`, a Node server function)
chunks.text:
- **Website import:** fetch the page on the server, then look for schema.org `Recipe` JSON-LD first, which is free and exact. Claude then only normalises it (aisles, canonical names, timers, GF check). If there's no JSON-LD, the cleaned page text goes to Claude to extract the recipe.
- **Instagram:** Instagram blocks scraping, so this takes two routes. First, try the public caption (og:description) from the link. If that fails, the screen asks you to paste the caption or add screenshots, which go to Claude vision. Links arrive through the "Send to GRKN" iOS Shortcut or by pasting.
- **Cookbook photos:** stored in Convex, then 1–4 page images are sent to Claude vision in a single request.

chunks.section: Claude integration (`convex/ai.ts`, a Node server function)
chunks.text:
- **Overlap planner:** takes the saved recipes' canonical ingredient lists plus the constraints. Claude returns a week of existing recipe IDs and new generated recipes. The server then works out the actual overlap score itself rather than trusting the model's count.
- **Weekly brief planner** (`claude-sonnet-5`, one call per week):
  - **Inputs:** the brief (proteins, theme, targets), the in-season list for this region and month (from `seasonalProduce`), compact titles, cuisines and proteins from the last 3 weeks' plans (to avoid repeating them), saved recipe ingredient lists, and the pantry's "use soon" items.

chunks.section: Claude integration (`convex/ai.ts`, a Node server function)
chunks.text:
- **Output:** a structured result per slot (an existing recipe ID or a short new-recipe card), with a nutrition estimate per serving. Each slot is written to `planDrafts` as it arrives.
  - **Targets are soft:** they're passed to Claude as recommendations. The server only works out the estimates for the indicators and never forces a retry.
  - **Actions on a single slot:**
    - **Replace:** one small call, given the kept meals as context.
    - **Edit in words:** a Haiku call that revises that one recipe from your instruction.
    - **Regenerate the rest:** one call covering only the slots that aren't kept.
    - **Your own or imported recipe:** reuses the Import pipeline, and the result is saved straight into the slot.

chunks.section: Claude integration (`convex/ai.ts`, a Node server function)
chunks.text:
- **Full recipes on demand:** as with Generate, full recipes are written only for new cards you keep, which keeps output tokens low.
- **Prep planner** (`claude-sonnet-5`, one call per plan):
  - **Inputs:** only the kept meals, each sent in a compact form (recipe ID, date and slot, ingredients with amounts, step text, `makeAhead` and fridge-life days), plus the prep day and the gluten status.
  - **Output:** structured `prepPlans`, where each task names the meal slots and step IDs it covers.
  - **Server checks:** every task must point at real meals and steps. The server also recomputes each meal's "eaten on" day against the storage days Claude gives, and moves anything that would be too old into the midweek top-up.

chunks.section: Claude integration (`convex/ai.ts`, a Node server function)
chunks.text:
- **Updating:** "Update prep plan" regenerates the plan but keeps tasks you've already ticked.
- **Breakfast generation** uses the same Generate flow with a meal-type selector. Breakfast cards are kept short, and make-ahead breakfasts get `makeAhead` and fridge-life days.
- **Seasonal suggestions:** the "In season now" strip, the Generate toggle and the Recipes filter all read `seasonalProduce`, so they don't cost an AI call. The table is created with one Haiku call per region the first time, then reviewed in Settings.
- **Nutrition accuracy:** protein and fibre are estimates. The recipe page labels them "≈ estimated", and portion sizes of the protein are stated in grams so the numbers can be checked.

Uses the week's plan entries × a scale factor (planned servings ÷ recipe servings) → combines ingredients by `canonical` → converts units where the family matches (g/kg, ml/l, tsp/tbsp/cup) and otherwise keeps separate lines → leaves out `staples` → matches the result against the existing items: sources get updated, ticked and manual items are kept, and items no longer needed from any recipe are removed. Kept as pure functions in `lib/ingredients.ts` so they can be unit tested.

chunks.section: Keeping the build efficient (Claude Code token use)
chunks.text:
- **Generate code with tools:** use official generators (`create-next-app`, `npx convex dev`, `shadcn add`, `@convex-dev/auth` init) instead of writing boilerplate by hand.
- **No subagents,** and only one browser check per milestone. Read screen state as text rather than screenshots, unless it's a visual check.
- **Write each file once.** Make targeted edits after that, don't reread files that were just written, and keep shell output short with `--silent` or `tail` on installs and builds.
- **Reuse over custom:** shadcn components for the UI, Convex's own optimistic-update helpers, the `web-push` library, and schema.org parsing with a small hand-written extractor (no heavy scraping libraries).

chunks.section: Keeping the build efficient (Claude Code token use)
chunks.text:
- **Small milestones:** each build step ends with a quick check (typecheck + relevant tests), so errors are caught early rather than debugged across the whole app.
- **Short commit messages** and no long explanations between steps. I'll report in at the end of each milestone.
Leftovers and batch cooking (one cook fills two slots), aisle order per store, a durable offline outbox, and AI images.

Convex (free), Vercel (free), Anthropic API key, Resend (free, for magic links), Google OAuth client (optional). I'll generate the VAPID keys for push notifications. Your region is needed for "in season"; it gets set in Settings.

- **Unit tests (Vitest):** `lib/ingredients.ts` combining and unit conversion; timer detection from step text; the rule that `glutenFree` is derived from `glutenRisk`.
- **Gluten checks:** a fixed set of 10 prompts and imports (including soy sauce, stock, oats and beer batter) must come back with the correct `glutenRisk` flags. This set is re-run whenever the prompts change.
- **Weekly brief checks:** a brief of salmon + chicken uses both, puts an in-season vegetable in every dinner, and shares no recipe titles with the previous week's plan. The protein and fibre indicators show and update correctly.

- **Breakfast checks:** turning breakfast on and off shows and hides the rows. A breakfast repeated Mon–Fri adds the right total amounts to the shopping list (5 servings), and editing it changes all the linked days.
- **Prep plan checks:** a week with salmon on Thursday must not prep the salmon on Sunday. Every task links to a meal that's actually kept. Changing a kept meal marks the plan "Meals changed". Ticking a task on one phone shows on the other within about 1 second.

- **Planning board checks:** keep 2 meals then "Regenerate the rest", and the kept meals stay unchanged. Edit a meal in words and only that slot changes. Replace a meal with a library recipe and with an imported link. With two sessions open on the same draft, each person's edits to different slots appear for the other within about 1 second.
- **Push notifications:** both installed iPhones receive a partner-change message and a locked-screen timer alert.
- **Real-phone check after milestone 2:** install on both iPhones from the Vercel URL, and confirm the shopping list syncs and feels native before any more features are built.

- **Convex function tests (`convex-test`):** rebuilding the list keeps checked and manual items; both of you calling `setChecked` at the same time ends up correct; household access rules (one household can't read another's data).
- **iPhone layout test (Playwright WebKit with the iPhone 15/SE device profiles):** no sideways scrolling, the tab bar clears the home indicator, tap targets are at least 44px, and text fields are at least 16px. This runs on every milestone.
- **Two-person sync test (Playwright):** two browser sessions logged in as different members. A ticks, B sees it within about 1s. Both tick different items at the same time. B goes offline, ticks, comes back, and A receives it.

- **Manual checks:** install the app on both phones from the Vercel URL, then do a real shop together; generate a GF recipe and a non-GF one; import one website, one Instagram post and one cookbook photo; run cook mode with 2 timers at once.

This source describes a small local web application designed to assist users during a live 12-team, full-PPR snake fantasy football draft on Sleeper. The main goal of the tool is to provide real-time pick tracking and recommendations based on expert consensus rankings.

- A small local web app ran alongside a live Sleeper fantasy football draft. ([[raw/Draft Copilot|Draft Copilot.md]])
- The app tracked every pick in real time and recommended who to take next. ([[raw/Draft Copilot|Draft Copilot.md]])
- The goal was a tool to use during a 12-team, full-PPR snake draft on Sleeper. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Objective|§ Objective]])
- Recommendations should come from expert consensus rankings, not Sleeper's ADP. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Objective|§ Objective]])
- The default rankings blend FantasyPros consensus and ESPN Field Yates PPR rankings. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Rankings dataset|§ Rankings dataset]])

- A player on both lists gets FantasyPros_rank × 0.6 + ESPN_rank × 0.4, and the list is re-sorted by that blended score. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Rankings dataset|§ Rankings dataset]])
- The app fetches picks every 3 seconds. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Features|§ Features]])
- Sleeper's CDN caches the picks endpoint for up to 30 seconds. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Features|§ Features]])
- My Team and Needs tracker automatically detects your own picks and slots them into starting slots. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Features|§ Features]])
- Check for an API before building scraping or screenshot reading. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Lessons|§ Lessons]])

- A screenshot app was rejected because reading text from images is unreliable. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Choosing the architecture|§ Choosing the architecture]])
- The live companion was the easier option because Sleeper has a public, no-login JSON API for drafts. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Choosing the architecture|§ Choosing the architecture]])
- Best Available shows consensus rankings with anyone already drafted by any team removed. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Features|§ Features]])

- Raw consensus rank answers who is the better player, but not who is the better pick right now. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#The Value Model|§ The Value Model]])
- The value model adds position scarcity as a secondary nudge to the raw consensus rank. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#The Value Model|§ The Value Model]])
- The first version used `replacement_rank − position_rank` alone. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#How the model evolved|§ How the model evolved]])
- This first version answered the 2.10 question by favoring the RB11 over the TE1, but it let scarcity override real differences in talent. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#How the model evolved|§ How the model evolved]])

- The 'My Team' empty in mock drafts bug was caused by Sleeper leaving `roster_id` null on mock-draft picks. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Bugs Found and Fixed|§ Bugs Found and Fixed]])
- The fix for the 'My Team' empty in mock drafts bug was to identify picks by `draft_slot`, which is set in both mock and real drafts. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Bugs Found and Fixed|§ Bugs Found and Fixed]])
- Test on a mock draft before relying on the app live. ([[raw/Draft Copilot#Lessons|§ Lessons]])

- [[Expert Consensus Rankings]]: Recommendations are derived from expert consensus rankings rather than Sleeper's standard ADP.
- [[API Pre-Check]]: The process involves checking for an API before attempting to build scraping or screenshot reading solutions.
- [[Caching]]: Sleeper's CDN caches the picks endpoint for up to 30 seconds, which the application leverages.
